title: Read the Priority Matrix
subtitle: Impact x urgency, not vibes
scenario: Priority is not how loud the customer is - it is a governed grid. Read Relay's impact-by-urgency matrix and understand how it derives P1 to P4, so an angry customer with low impact does not jump the queue.
input:
Relay's priority matrix (owned by the Support Ops Analyst, v1.0.0) maps impact x urgency to a priority:
- high impact + high urgency = P1
- high impact + low urgency = P2
- low impact + high urgency = P3
- low impact + low urgency = P4
Impact = how many/how badly affected. Urgency = how fast it must move. Priority is derived, not felt.
instructions: Read the matrix as owned config that derives priority from impact and urgency.
Answer the four questions about derivation, the P1 boundary, and ownership.
Validate to mint the priority-matrix record.

questions.prompt: How is a ticket's priority decided?

options.text: By how upset the customer sounds
By looking up impact x urgency in the matrix

questions.explain: Priority is derived from the matrix: impact (how many/how badly) crossed with urgency (how fast). Tone is not an input.

questions.prompt: An angry customer reports a typo on a help page. What priority?

options.text: P4 - low impact, low urgency, no matter the tone
P2 - anger raises it one level

questions.explain: Low impact + low urgency = P4. The matrix protects the P1 queue from emotion; a typo is not an outage.

options.text: High impact AND high urgency together
The customer asking for a manager

questions.explain: P1 is the top-left cell: high impact and high urgency. One high value alone is P2 or P3, not P1.

questions.prompt: Who owns changes to the matrix?

options.text: The Support Ops Analyst, and changes are versioned

questions.explain: The Support Ops Analyst owns the matrix and versions changes, so priority stays consistent and auditable.

copilotPrompt: Explain a support priority matrix: priority is impact x urgency looked up in a governed grid (not tone), P1 requires both high, an angry low-impact ticket is still P4, and the Support Ops Analyst owns versioned changes.
successMessage: Matrix read. Priority is a lookup, not a feeling - the P1 queue is protected.

sections.title: Priority is derived
sections.body: A matrix crosses impact (how many, how badly) with urgency (how fast) to yield P1-P4. Deriving priority from two named inputs is what makes it defensible instead of a gut call.

sections.title: The P1 boundary matters most
sections.body: P1 is expensive - it pages people. The matrix guards it: only high impact AND high urgency qualify. An angry customer with a typo is a P4, and the grid says so in writing.

sections.title: Config, owned and versioned
sections.body: The matrix is owned by the Support Ops Analyst and versioned. When the mix of priorities drifts, you change the config, not the individual calls.

sections.title: What you produce here
sections.body: A priority-matrix record the assignment step applies to every ticket.

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: You'd keep a simple impact-by-urgency grid and look up every ticket's priority in it, rather than rating by how the ticket sounds.

tools.zapier: a table mapping the two inputs to a priority

takeaway.heading: Matrix read
points: Priority is impact x urgency looked up in a governed grid, not tone.
P1 requires both high impact and high urgency.
An angry, low-impact ticket is still a P4 - the grid protects P1.
The Support Ops Analyst owns versioned changes to the matrix.
The workflow can now derive a defensible priority for every ticket.
